utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-72-A, the Prosecutor versus Milan Babic, appeals hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to make sure that the interpreters are in place and can hear us and we can also hear them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now have the parties. The Defence, as the appellants, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam President, Your Honours. Mr. Robert Fogelnest and Peter Michael Mueller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Mark McKeon, with my co-counsel Mr. Xavier Tracol and Ms. Kristina Carey. And we are also accompanied in this Chambers by our case manager, Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I would like to find out whether the accused -- the appellant Mr. Milan Babic, can hear the proceedings in a language he understands, please. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. I would like to explain how we are going to proceed during this hearing. As the Registrar announced, the case on our agenda is that of the Prosecutor versus Milan Babic. As this is an appeal Mr. Milan Babic is the appellant. This is an appeal from a judgement rendered by the Trial Chamber on 29th June 2004. At a plea hearing held on the 27th of January, 2004, Mr. Babic, the appellant, pleaded guilty to one count of persecution, arising out of events that took place in Croatia, where he participated in a joint criminal enterprise that came into existence from 1 August 1991 and continued until at least June 1992. The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was the permanent forcible removal of the majority of the Croat and other non-Serb population from approximately one-third of the territory of Croatia in order to make it part of a new Serb-dominated state through the commission of crimes in violation of Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal. These areas included those regions that were referred to by Serb authorities as the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina; the Serbian Autonomous District of Western Slavonia; the Serbian Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. After 19th December 1991, the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina became known as the Republic of Serbia, Serbian Krajina. On 26th February, 1992, the Serbian Autonomous District of Western Slavonia and the Serbian Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem joined the Republic of Serbian Krajina as well as the Dubrovnik Republic. On 28 January 2004, based on a plea agreement filed on the 22nd January 2004, the Trial Chamber entered a conviction under Articles 5(h) and 7(1) of the Tribunal's statute against Mr. Babic -- I want to find out whether we have a problem. I understand the transcript is not working. Are we still having a problem? I understand the microphone is working. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you please slow down for the interpretation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'll go back a bit. On 28 January 2004, based on a plea agreement filed on 22 January 2004, the Trial Chamber entered a conviction under Articles 5(h) and 7(1) of the Tribunal's statute against Mr. Babic on Count 1 of the indictment issued on the 6th of November 2003, for persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, for his participation in the joint criminal enterprise as a co-perpetrator. The Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Babic to 13 years of imprisonment on 29 June 2004. Mr. Babic has now appealed. This morning, we will hear submissions on appeal from both parties, but before giving the floor to counsel, I will summarise briefly the appellant's grounds of appeal as stated in the written submissions. When filing his notice of appeal on 3rd September 2004, Mr. Babic initially raised 12 grounds of appeal. On 15th November 2004, he withdrew ground of appeal number 12. The first ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion by coercing Mr. Babic to enter a plea of guilt as a co-perpetrator and by declining to accept the first plea agreement in which he was to plead guilty as an aider and abettor. The second ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to issue a reasoned opinion as required under Article 23 of the Statute. In his third ground of appeal, Mr. Babic argues that the Trial Chamber erred in failing to consider and weigh the evidence concerning his limited participation as a mitigating factor. In the fourth ground of appeal, Mr. Babic contends that the Trial Chamber erred in failing to afford appropriate weight as a mitigating circumstance to the fact that he and his family must continue to live as protected witnesses. In the fifth ground of appeal, Mr. Babic argues that the Trial Chamber erred in failing to consider his prior good conduct as a mitigating circumstance. In the sixth ground of appeal, Mr. Babic asserts that the Trial Chamber erred in failing to consider his conduct subsequent to the crime as a mitigating circumstance. In the seventh ground of appeal the appellant argues that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion in finding that he held a leadership position and in considering that as an aggravating factor. The eighth ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber grossly misconstrued Mr. Babic's role and his participation in the joint criminal enterprise. In the ninth ground of appeal, Mr. Babic argues that the Trial Chamber erred by basing its decision on facts that occurred outside the temporal scope of the indictment. The tenth ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber failed to afford appropriate weight to the totality of mitigating circumstances that it found had been established. Finally, as the eleventh ground of appeal, Mr. Babic argues that the Trial Chamber erred in imposing a burden upon him to convince it of his recognition of the significance of his own role in Croatia during that period. I would now like to remind the parties about the standard of review applicable to sentencing appeals. The relevant provisions on sentencing are Articles 23 and 24 of the Statute and Rules 100 to 106 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under Article 25 of the Statute, an appeal is not a trial de novo; the role of the Appeals Chamber is limited to correcting errors of law, invalidating a decision and errors of fact that have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Trial Chambers have a wide discretion when exercising their powers of sanction and penalty so as to fit individual circumstances of the accused and the gravity of the crime. The Rules of Procedure -- the rules of practice are that the Appeals Chamber will not revise a sentence unless it is demonstrated that the Trial Chamber committed a discernable error in exercising its discretion. A Trial Chamber's decision may, for example, be disturbed on appeal if the appellant shows that the Trial Chamber erred in the weighing process either by taking into account what it ought not to have considered or by failing to take into account what it tut have taken into account. As we proceed, I would also ask the parties to be precise and clear in their submissions and to observe time. Consistent with our scheduling order which was issued some time ago, the appellant has up to 30 minutes to make the submissions on the appeal. The Prosecution will have 30 minutes to respond to the appellant's submissions, and the appellant, if he so wishes, will have ten minutes to reply. The appellant will have ten minutes to reply to the Prosecution's response. If there are no questions from the outset, we will proceed hearing counsel. But before we start I would like to make clear to the appellant that at the end of the submissions by counsel, he may address the Appeals Chamber for ten minutes if he so wishes. He may also raise any matters concerning his conditions of detention and his health, if he so wishes. I'll just find out whether there are any queries from my colleagues. I see none. I'll call upon counsel for the appellant to address the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, distinguished learned colleagues, I would like to say right away at the beginning that I carefully read the last scheduling order issued by the appellant -- Appeals Chamber. Recounting what has been submitted in writing already earlier is indeed superfluous and in addition to this, it would be also unpolite, for it would insinuate that the submissions were not taken note of. In addition to this, Your Honours, I can announce that I will not exhaust the period of time allocated to the appellant, Defence. First, let me make one point which struck me right at the beginning of today's hearing when I read the transcript on the screen on the very first page in line 8. I might suggest that the wording there -- the joint criminal enterprise came into existence on August 1, 1991 and continued at least to June 1992 be amended, in that case into February 1992 because that is the date the indictment against Mr. Babic refers to. It's in paragraph 7 of the indictment, by the way. Thank you. I would like -- Your Honours, I would like to deal with the submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you start I just wanted to take note of that amendment because the indictment is clear as to the period of the indictment which is covered. The description of the events may be different but the indictment is clear for the period covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: The indictment is clear, as it says, until at least February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: If you consider this to be sufficient, I agree, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I would like to deal with the submission of the Office of the Prosecutor dated 20 December 2004, just very, very cursorily. Appellant and Prosecution have presented their points of view very clearly and the only issues I would like to raise at this occasions are these ones. The Prosecution concurs with the appellant with respect to the grounds of appeal number 3, 5 and 6, and the appellant joins these arguments in addition to his own ones in this context. All the rest of the grounds submitted by appellant were requested to be dismissed. I have to admit very frankly, Your Honours, that I were [sic] very happy if the Prosecution could have met the position taken by the appellant regarding grounds 7 and 9 in a more favourable way. But with respect to grounds 1, 2, 4, 8, 10 and 11, the Prosecution's arguments are received with greatest respect, they are comprehensible sine ira et studio although appellant's position is a little different. Let me come back to ground 7 and 9 and let me deal with it in an antinumerical order, ground number 9 first and very briefly. The Prosecution concludes in its submission in paragraph 3.86, starting at the fourth line from below, read as a whole, the judgement suggests that the Trial Chamber was fully aware of the geographic and temporal limits of the appellant's participation and ruled accordingly. Accordingly the Trial Chamber did not make a discernable error in validating the judgement. My remark on this very occasion is just this one, that appellant's impression is that the wording of the judgement suggests the contrary. The scope of appellant's influence, his sphere of control never ever covered one-third of Croatia's territory. Therefore, the verdict of the judgement remains at least unclear and lacks this level of clarity which is needed when handing down a judgement. With respect to the seventh ground of appeal, I would like to make reference to paragraphs 3.68 and 3.50 of Prosecution's response. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Prosecution came to the conclusion that the appellant, and I quote 3.68, "That the appellant has mischaracterised the Trial Chamber's holding with respect to the appellant's leading role," and the submission continues by saying "the Trial Chamber never concluded that the appellant had a leadership role in the joint criminal enterprise." A footnote, number 131, in that submission of Prosecution, is attached to this conclusion and this footnote refers to paragraph 79 of the sentencing judgement. Which reads as follows -- this source reads as follows: It's the fourth line from below, paragraph 79 of the judgement, "Babic's role in the JCE allowed the JCE to function; his participation furthered the objective of the JCE." I do not read there Babic -- "Babic's role as a high-level political leader allowed the JCE to function;". The wording is as I quoted before. It must be clear, Your Honours, that by applying an argumentum in contrarium, this wording of the judgement very clearly does not mean anything else than without Babic the JCE would not have functioned as it did. What else, Your Honours, does this insinuate and mean than that Babic was a key factor in the JCE or did have a leadership role? This is why we cannot follow the submissions of the Prosecution in that context. And as a consequence of that, what I have placed on your table now, one must come to the following conclusions, to my opinion. First, it is not accurate when the Prosecution emphasises that the Trial Chamber never concluded that the appellant had a leadership role in the JCE; and second, and even more important, the way how the Trial Chamber dealt with the earlier submissions of the parties, the evaluation of these submissions, such as exempli gratia, the factual statement, the sentencing briefs and the evidence submitted jointly by OTP and the Defence to the Trial Chamber, might have been erroneous. I intentionally use the subjunctive wording "might have been erroneous," because in this very moment of my arguments, I feel compelled to introduce here and - now a general observation on the subject of clarity and elimination of potential errors in judgements - in case a judgement's wording leaves room for interpretation, it cannot be characterised as unambiguous. Thus, it lacks of a certain level of ultimate clarity which, however, is needed to rule out the potential error on the side of a Trial Chamber. Uncertainty -- uncertainty is thus one of the different levels of the term "error." And please allow me to refer to my personal experience, which I have in that context in Germany, the country I'm from. Such unclear verdicts always lead to the Federal High Court of Justice reversing the judgement at issue. The reasons given for the reversal is that it cannot be established beyond all doubt whether or not a Chamber acted unerroneously. This lack of clarity, Your Honours, of the judgement of the Trial Chamber has already been examined in appellant's brief of appeal and my oral submissions here of today took this -- took up this issue again briefly. This lack of charity also has been carved out in part by relevant arguments contained in the Prosecution's response, and I would like to emphasise inter alia paragraph 3.46 of the Prosecution's response in that context. I do not intend to quote that any longer. Madam President, Your Honours, please let me conclude by requesting these Appeals Chamber to allow therefore the submitted grounds and to revise the sentence handed down by the Trial Chamber accordingly. And as you can see, I have strictly obeyed your scheduling order and I thank you very much for your kind attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. I'll just find out if there are questions. Judge Guney wishes to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam President. I do have a question that I'd like to address the Defence counsel with regard to the eleventh ground of appeal. Do you think that the judgement by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 98 of the sentencing judgement according to which the appellant did not always at all times recognise the significance of the part and the role he played in Croatia, do you think that this has been considered by the Trial Chamber as a circumstance that would be an aggravating circumstance? If it is so, how do you account for the fact that the Trial Chamber did not mention this element in the part of the judgement dealing with the aggravating circumstances in the sentencing judgement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour? I can't see all of you, I apologise. Let me see if I can -- how is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Come right here, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel may have to take the other podium.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: My apologies. The problem is, it's very confusing. In their opinion, they speak of him not fully recognising what his role was. However, from all of the statements in the factual basis and from all of the statements given to the Trial Chamber by the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Babic did recognise and was remorseful and accepted responsibility. He went to the Tribunal before he was indicted. He cooperated and testified against Milosevic for, I believe, 18 days, before he was indicted. He did all of this while under witness security, knowing that he was to be indicted. He testified subsequently, after he had entered his plea of guilty. He expressed his remorse at the time he entered his plea. All of these things belie the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he did not recognise the significance of his acts. So I have no explanation for why they said that. Does that answer Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Fogelnest?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Is there another question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: This question is addressed to Mr. Fogelnest. I have been perplexed so why the Trial Chamber made no reference, in its sentencing judgement, to the appellant's involvement in the peace negotiations. I am speaking of your sixth ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Yes, the conversations with Peter Galbraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. There doesn't seem to be any reference in the judgement to that aspect, and I am interrogating myself as to why this might be. I have before me your sentencing brief before the Trial Chamber, and in that sentencing brief, paragraph 65, of which deals with conduct subsequent to the crime, there I would have expected to see some reference to this matter, but no reference was made there in that paragraph. I'm talking only of your written -- written arguments before the Trial Chamber. I see that in your appeal brief, appellant's brief before this Chamber, dated 15th of January 2004, you said in paragraph 132, the Trial Chamber was presented -- was presented -- with evidence that Peter Galbraith, the American ambassador to Croatia, met the appellant in 1955 [sic] in connection with the Z-4 peace plan negotiations, and then you refer in footnote 99 to the Prosecutor's sentencing brief in which, no doubt, the Prosecution developed that aspect of the matter. But it seems to me that the appellant himself, in his written arguments before the Trial Chamber, did not refer to these peace plan negotiations or to his involvement in them. Could you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, candidly, I think we were negligent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: That should have been in the brief. It was not. However, the Trial Chamber was presented with all of the transcripts from the Milosevic trial, including those of Peter Galbraith. I believe the Prosecution mentioned it in their brief and I confess negligence in not mentioning it in ours. This was a rather overwhelming task and I apologise but that's the honest answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, that satisfies all the tests referred to by your distinguished colleague when he spoke of the necessity for clarity. I accept your statement that it was an oversight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Are there any other questions, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just as a follow-up question to this. Apparently, the Trial Chamber addressed there question in paragraphs 95, 96, when discussing the subsequent conduct of the appellant by saying that "the Trial Chamber is not satisfied that conclusive evidence was provided that Babic alleviated the suffering of victims whether immediately after the commission of the crime... or after the end of the armed conflict... His subsequent behaviour concerned matters such as cooperation and acceptance of responsibility, which have already been considered. "The Trial Chamber rejects the Defence's claims that Babic's post-conflict conduct constitutes a mitigating circumstance." I'm extremely grateful to my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, having already addressed this question. Could you please give me some further guidance where the Trial Chamber could have found when rendering the sentencing judgement additional arguments, either in the transcript or in the plea agreement, on this post-crime conduct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: If I understand your question, Judge Schomburg, I believe it's answered in the brief in that there is a two-pronged argument. The first is that -- well, that the -- Mr. Babic must provide conclusive evidence. For a mitigating factor, it is only by a preponderance of the evidence, not by conclusive evidence. The second prong is that the -- alleviating the suffering of the victims is only but one factor in this area which could be considered. The problem is that they did not address at all Mr. Babic's participation in the Z-4 discussions with Ambassador Galbraith. I hope that answers your question, Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this, and let me continue with two questions I in principle should not put to you because they are hypothetical by nature. Please allow me to ask them. In case when you had the first meetings with the Prosecution and the Prosecution would have offered to you a plea agreement describing the criminal conduct of your -- of the appellant as co-perpetrator and not as an aider and abettor, would this have been an obstacle to you to enter a plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: It's a heck of a question. I'm not certain. Here is the problem. The distinction between aider and abettor and a level 3 co-perpetrator is, in all candour, barely comprehensible. Let me -- I beg your indulgence. In Tadic, there were three different categories of mens rea engendering culpability as a co-perpetrator in a JCE. The third category of cases arises where there is a state of mind in which a person, although he did not intend to bring about a certain result, was aware that the actions of the group were most likely to lead to that result but nevertheless willingly took the risk. In the Blaskic appeal and Vasiljevic, in the case of aiding and abetting, the requisite mental element is "knowledge that the acts performed by the aider and abettor assist in the commission of a specific crime of the principal." Those two are very difficult to discern the difference. Would it have presented a problem? Probably, but I can't say for certain. Here was the situation, Judge Schomburg: Babic came forward when he saw his name on a Milosevic indictment, cooperated with the Tribunal, cooperated with the OTP. It was a fait accompli that he would be indicted and plead guilty. So should he have pled guilty as an aider and abetter? Should he have pled guilty as a co-perpetrator, given these definitions? I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this extremely honest answer, because I would also have my difficulties to see a discernable distinction between these two heads of responsibility. But the final question would be: When, from the outset the agreement would have been based on the suggestions by the Prosecution that the outcome -- be it now aiding and abetting, be it now the third category of joint criminal enterprise -- that the outcome should be 13 years. And this is a question of -- also of remorse and accepting guilt and showing people on the ground that, in fact, your client feels responsible for these crimes. I don't want to minimise two years. Two years in life is a lot. However, would at that time this have been an obstacle for you to entering a plea agreement if the result would have been of the plea agreement 13 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: That again is difficult for me to answer because knowing now what I know about the effect of a plea agreement - which is nothing - it probably would not have been, to be honest with you. However, at the time, we believed that a plea agreement meant something, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the Court would be guided by a plea agreement, that they would follow the recommendation. We understand that the Statute provides that they need not do so. But we thought that at least, if there was a violation of the plea agreement -- it's not the right word -- but if there was a disqualification of the plea agreement, that the Court would at least explain its reasons in a way that would make sense. Clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Are there any other questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see none. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Mumba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I now call upon the Prosecution to respond. 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This morning, to the extent that it's necessary to actually make oral submissions on the various grounds of appeal, my co-counsel, Ms. Kristina Carey will be addressing the first, third, seventh, eighth and ninth grounds of appeal. Mr. Tracol will be addressing the fourth, fifth, sixth, tenth and eleventh ground of appeal, and I will be addressing the second ground of appeal. For those grounds of appeal where we don't make oral submissions, then we will of course be available to answer any questions that you might have on those various grounds. Before we get into the substantive arguments, I did want to clarify one part of our brief which I think left a question unanswered, which is: If the Appeals Chamber accepts our submission that there were errors in some of the grounds of appeal or indeed their suggestion that other grounds of appeal had errors, what is the Prosecution's recommendation now on what sentence is appropriate for Mr. Babic. We didn't address that in our brief. As you know, at the Trial Chamber, our recommendation was that Mr. Babic should receive a sentence of less than 11 years. And we emphasised in the Trial Chamber below 11 years. As you've pointed out to us at the beginning of this hearing and as we say in our submissions, of course, the mere fact that the Trial Chamber did not follow our recommendation does not mean that there was a discernible error and that the judgement should be revised. Therefore, we've carefully gone through the arguments made by the appellant, disagreed where we must with those submissions which we think are legally wrong, and agreed where we must with those where we think there was error. Our submission is that if you agree with the appellant and with us that there was legal error in the third, fifth and sixth of ground appeal, or indeed in any of the other grounds of appeal, that the appropriate sentence is the one that we recommended before the Trial Chamber, which is a sentence below 11 years of imprisonment. With that, Your Honour, I would like to without further delay turn the podium over to my colleague, Ms. Kristina Carey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Carey.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Briefly, before turning to my grounds of appeal, I would like to address some of the points that were raised by my learned colleagues for the appellant. With respect to ground 7, I would just like to highlight that paragraph 79 which was pointed out in our brief does not deal with the aggravating circumstance that was in question but in fact deals with mitigating circumstances. Also, paragraph 79 indicates that the Trial Chamber understood that the appellant was not, to quote this -- to quote the judgement, "the prime mover in the campaign of persecutions." I would point the Appeals Chamber to paragraphs 54 and 62, which do deal with aggravating circumstances, and in that -- in those paragraphs, the Trial Chamber focused on his position as a high-level political leader, and I will address this -- the ground in its entirety a little bit further on, unless you have questions now. With respect to ground 9, I would first like to point out that my learned colleague stated something in the order of if there might have been an error, then this Chamber must reverse ground 9. That is in fact not the standard of review. The appellant is required to show that there was a discernible error and in this case, they did not do so. Specifically with respect to some of their additional arguments in ground 9, the indictment clearly differentiates between the goal of the joint criminal enterprise itself and the temporal and geographic scope of the appellant's own participation in the joint criminal enterprise. In this particular case, the Trial Chamber adopted the very language that was used in the indictment with respect to the scope of the JCE and the scope of the appellant's participation. This is the indictment to which this appellant pled. In a complete reading of the judgement, you can see that the Trial Chamber did, when talking about the actual conduct of the appellant, limit itself to the area located in the Krajina and the time period between the 1st of August 1991 and the 15th of February 1992. And I would like to specifically point Your Honours to the paragraphs in the sentencing judgement, paragraphs -- you don't need to read them right now but the paragraphs 14, 15, 50 and 51. Now, with that, I would like to move on to my -- the grounds that I have prepared this morning. One of the critical questions in this appeal is whether the Trial Chamber made an error with respect to its characterisation of the appellant's overall criminal conduct. The appellant in this respect has raised four grounds that attempt to identify an error. These grounds are ground 1, ground 3, ground 7 and ground 8. As my co-counsel has indicated, and as our learned colleagues have indicated, there is a ground upon which we agree, and that is ground 3. The Prosecution believes that it is in this ground where one can indicate, one can see an error made by the Trial Chamber that has impacted the sentence and feels that this error is best characterised by the Trial Chamber or in is best characterised as one being -- concerning the gravity of the offence. The Prosecution disagrees based solely upon the law with the appellant's other three grounds with relation to this issue which are grounds 1, 7 and 8. I would like to go first to ground 3, which is the ground upon which we are in agreement with the appellant. The Trial Chamber did make a legal error with respect to the gravity of the offence. The Trial Chamber failed to an adequately consider the form and nature of the appellant's participation in the crimes that were charged. This led them to impose an excessive sentence. The gravity of the offence is the starting point for determining sentence. It requires that the Trial Chamber consider the form and degree of the participation of the accused in the crime. In this particular case, the Trial Chamber determined that the appellant's participation was sufficient to make him a co-perpetrator rather than an aider and abettor. The Trial Chamber, as you have been -- as our colleagues have -- our learned colleagues for the appellant have indicated, disagreed with both the Prosecution and the Defence at trial as to the -- whether or not his participation was sufficiently limited to construe -- to constitute a mitigating circumstance. The Trial Chamber, however, did not consider his participation in light of the entire scope of the criminality of the joint criminal enterprise in this case, or in comparison with the participation of his fellow co-perpetrators. The appellant's participation was far less extensive than his fellow co-perpetrators in this case. He did not physically perpetrate any of the underlying crimes. He also did not command the physical perpetrators. He was also, as indicated in the plea agreement and factual statement, marginalised by those high-level players in the joint criminal enterprise, diminishing his ability to take action. The Prosecution submits that for the reasons that are set out here and also in our brief, that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to consider these critical facts and because of that, it did not adequately consider the participation of the accused when it came to a conclusion about the gravity of the offence. Unless Your Honours have questions, I would like to move to ground 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There are no questions. Counsel, you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: With respect to the first ground of appeal the Trial Chamber did not err when it indicated that the legal qualification of Mr. Babic as an aider and abettor was inconsistent with some of the facts that were presented in the factual statement. At all times, the Trial Chamber acted within the confines of the critical Rule, which is Rule 62 bis(4). That requires the Trial Chamber be satisfied with the totality of an accused's criminal conduct, that it's reflected in the plea agreement before they may accept that plea. Even in this case, where the parties agreed, the Trial Chamber must still satisfy itself that the accused is guilty of the crimes charged in the indictment and that it encompasses the full, the totality of his criminal conduct when the Trial Chamber evaluates the materials before it. In this case, the Trial Chamber indicated that the facts that were in the factual statement that led the Trial Chamber to its view -- or that there were factual -- things within the factual statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. In this case, the Trial Chamber did indicate that there were facts contained in the factual summary that led it to its conclusion that the aiding and abetting was not a proper characterisation. Now, it's important also at this critical stage that the Appeals Chamber feel confident that the conviction as a co-perpetrator is safe. In this case, the -- meaning that the appellant entered the plea voluntarily, and with knowledge of the crimes that were charged and the distinction between the possible crimes that could have been convicted of. In this specific case, the Trial Chamber asked the appellant if he understood specifically the change in the plea between plea agreement 1 and plea agreement 2 and whether he understood the implications of this change in the further appearance and the appellant in this case said that he did. Also in the course of the plea agreement, the appellant confirmed that he was not going to later challenge his plea of guilty. While it's not now the Prosecution's understanding that that is the appellant's intent, if in fact the appellant is now indicating that somehow there was a problem with the understanding of the distinction between aiding and abetting and co-perpetration, that would go to the critical issues of whether or not he understood what he was pleading to and of course the remedy in that case would not be a reduction of sentence, which is what is being requested, but in fact an order for a new trial. There was a further point made in the appellant's first ground which was that the Trial Chamber erred by not allowing Mr. Babic to it enter an open plea. In this case an open plea isn't available under the Statute and is not appropriate. Also a Trial Chamber can only accept a plea from an accused who is fully apprised of the nature and consequences of his plea and to what precisely he is pleading guilty. In this case, an open plea would have made that impossible. Turning briefly to ground 7, I just want to re-emphasise here that the appellant -- in this particular ground, the appellant has misconstrued what the Trial Chamber did. It did not base this particular aggravating circumstance on Mr. Babic's leadership role in the joint criminal enterprise. In fact, it based the aggravating circumstance on his role as a regional political leader. There was a decision that is very well founded in Tribunal jurisprudence and in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the factors being considered aggravating in many cases including the case of Biljana Plavsic of Simic, Miroslav Deronjic and Kordic, amongst others. It's been well accepted and the Appeals Chamber itself has highlighted that this is one of the points upon which aggravating factor can be determined. And then just turning briefly to ground 9 -- actually, I'm not going to turn to ground 9. I feel that I've adequately covered that in my opening statement. And unless Your Honours have any other questions, I would conclude my presentation at this time and make time for my colleague, Mr. Tracol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, there are no questions. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CAREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, Your Honours, I am now going to reply to five grounds of appeal: ground 4, life as a protected witness; ground 5, good character, prior good character; ground 6, subsequent conduct to the commission of the crime; ground 10, insufficient weight according to Defence given to the totality of mitigating factors; and then briefly ground 11, raised by the appellant. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Most of these grounds have to do with mitigating circumstances. My colleague, McKeon, told you earlier on that the Prosecution agreed with the Defence on some of these grounds. I would like now to return to the reasons why we agreed on some grounds. Sometimes these reasons may differ from the grounds expressed by the appellant counsel. With regard to ground 4, namely life as a protected witness, the Prosecution first notes that this ground of appeal only deals with the appreciation or assessment of the weight given by the Trial Chamber to mitigating factors and not a distinct question, which is to identify what mitigating factors actually are. We do concede that the appellant is the first accused who was a protected witness to be relocated with the members of his family. In a way, he is a protected accused. As such, his situation is really, literally, extraordinary; it is out of the ordinary. According to the Prosecution, the appellant failed to discharge his burden of proof which was to show that the Trial Chamber made a discernible error by taking into account factors it ought not to have taken into account or by not taking into account elements that is it should have taken into account. This is why we think that ground 4 should be dismissed. On the one hand, the Trial Chamber did take into account the consequences of cooperation by the appellant for himself and for the members of his family. I now refer to paragraphs 3, 74, 87 and 88 of the sentencing judgement. These arguments were developed by the Prosecution in 3.51 of the brief. On the other hand, Trial Chambers are not legally required to describe what mitigating circumstances are, substantial or not. They are not legally required to describe them as substantial or not but this is precisely what the Trial Chamber did in this instant case, especially in paragraph 75, and I'm going to quote: "The Trial Chamber granted substantial weight to the cooperation by Milan Babic with the Tribunal." And this cooperation does include and entail his status as a protected witness. When all is said and done, the Trial Chamber did take into account his status as a protected witness but on two occasions in the judgement: When it looked into his cooperation with the Tribunal on the one hand; and on the other hand, when it considered his personal and the family circumstances. This being so, the appellant is in no position to claim that the Trial Chamber did not give sufficient weight to this mitigating factor. With regard to ground 5, dealing with prior good character, the Prosecution submits that it can be a mitigating factor but the weight given to this mitigating factor is generally of a limited scope, absent exceptional circumstances. In this case, the Trial Chamber in paragraph 91 of its sentencing judgement said the following: And I quote: "Prior good character of somebody convicted cannot be taken individually as a mitigating factor even though it may be so in exceptional circumstances, which was not established in this case." So the Prosecution submits that no great -- that the Trial Chamber held that no weight can be given absent exceptional circumstances. But the jurisprudence of the Tribunal only gives a limited weight to this mitigating factor absent exceptional circumstances. Therefore it is quite different, in as much the ruling of the Trial Chamber is inconsistent with the case law of Trial Chambers in the Tribunal. According to the Prosecution, this inconsistency - and of course, especially the way it was applied here - is a discernible error by the Trial Chamber. This is why the Prosecution respectfully requests revisement -- revision of the judgement and reduction of the sentence against the appellant on the basis of ground 5. With regard to ground 6, subsequent conduct to the commission of the crime, the Trial Chamber first considered in paragraph 94 of the judgement, "Conduct subsequent to the crime as a factor which has been accepted in other cases before the Tribunal where the convicted person acted immediately after the commission of the crime to alleviate the suffering of victims." Judge Schomburg mentioned this in his question earlier on. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber considered that the subsequent conduct is only relevant if he acts in such a way as to alleviate the suffering of victims. In doing so the Trial Chamber applied the wrong legal standards to the facts of the case. This is why the Prosecution also requests the Appeals Chamber to revise the judgement and to reduce the sentence handed down in the first instance. Secondly, the Trial Chamber also wrongly misinterpreted the sentencing judgement in the Plavsic case. Trial Chamber III looked into subsequent conduct and regarded it as a mitigating factor in the light of reconciliation, rather than alleviating the suffering of victims, paragraph 87 of the sentencing judgement in the Plavsic case. But here, in this instant case, these are parallel actions to those of Biljana Plavsic that the Trial Chamber did not even mention such actions by the appellant. Judge Shahabuddeen mentioned this earlier on. For instance, the appellant was the only one to attempt to reconcile with the Croats; he negotiated with them in order to arrive at a peaceful solution. He worked, he actively worked towards peace in the region. And I shall also note that the parties at Trial Chamber level did tender into evidence elements to go to show it, Exhibits PS5 and 6, which is the testimony by the Ambassador Galbraith in the Milosevic case and the transcript of Mr. Babic's testimony in the Milosevic case. This was expanded by the Prosecution in their brief it filed before the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 3.64, but this evidence was also before the Trial Chamber, which did not even mention such evidence, whilst it had it before it. The fact that the Trial Chamber neglected this evidence brings us to surmise that it did not take into account this element when it handed down its sentence. So the only conclusion possible is that the Trial Chamber very simply ignored this evidence and did not take it into account. But the Trial Chamber did recognise that parallel action by Biljana Plavsic was a mitigating circumstance. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber made a discernible error by making a distinction between the subsequent conduct by Plavsic and that of the appellant. As to the tenth ground of appeal which is insufficient weight granted to the totality of mitigating factors, the Prosecution submits that the appellant failed to prove that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion by not giving enough weight to mitigating factors, be they taken individually or in toto. This is why the Prosecution requests the Appeals Chamber to dismiss this tenth ground of appeal by the appellant. Now more specifically to remorse, which was mentioned before by Judge Schomburg. The appellant failed to prove that the Trial Chamber did not give enough weight to the remorse he showed. This being said, we do recognise and concede that the appellant's case is a unique one because he expressed his remorse whilst the Prosecution was still in its investigative phase. He's the only protected witness who is relocated and he was indicted before -- after he testified in a trial. With regard to the substantial and extensive cooperation, we note that in paragraph 75 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber gave substantial weight to his cooperation with the Tribunal in determining its sentence. Now, as to voluntary surrender, the Trial Chamber expressly took this into account in mitigation in paragraph 86 of the judgement and the appellant failed to show that the Trial Chamber would not have given enough weight to this mitigating factor. This being said, the appellant did know that he was going to be convicted to a term of imprisonment when he agreed to testify as a Prosecution witness in the Milosevic case, and to be relocated as a protected witness and this makes a clear distinction between his case and that of accused who have been indicted, arrested and then later on plead guilty. The chronology is quite different regarding Mr. Babic as to personal and family circumstances; the Trial Chamber did take them into account. I now refer to paragraphs 87 and 88 of the sentencing judgement. Finally, and I told you I was going to be brief, with regard to the eleventh ground of appeal to which Judge Guney referred earlier on. I think we have to go back to the appellant's brief in this case. What was claimed here is that the Trial Chamber would have considered that the appellant lied, did not tell the truth. This is not quite the -- what the Trial Chamber said. It never stated that it deemed that the accused did not tell the truth. It said that it was not satisfied, it said so towards the end of paragraph 98, as was stated by the Defence. It said that the appellant did not always fully recognise the relevance of the part he played in Croatia. This is quite a different conclusion. The Trial Chamber did not say that he lied. It never said that he never told the truth. It is not what the Trial Chamber said. I have finished and of course, I am at your disposal should you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah, there are no questions for you, Counsel. Thank you for your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm conscious of the time and so I will be very brief on ground 2. This is the ground that claims that the Trial Chamber did not give a reasoned opinion on two matters: One is that it didn't resolve certain undisputed matters of fact; and secondly, didn't explain the reasons why it rejected the Prosecution's sentencing recommendation. On the second one, second point, the only thing I want to do is to point out to the Appeals Chamber that after the filing of our brief there has been a development in the law on this second question and that's the Dragan Nikolic appeals decision. In the Dragan Nikolic case, the Appeals Chamber found that should the sentence diverge substantially from the plea agreement's recommendation, the Trial Chamber must give reasons for that departure. In the Nikolic case, I would point out the divergence in that case was 23 years versus 15 years, as opposed to in this case 13 years versus 11. So I would submit, first of all, that there hasn't been a substantial deviation from the plea agreement in our case. But secondly, even if there was, that the reasons given by the Trial Chamber did adequately explain why they rejected the Prosecution's recommendation, which is that they took a different view first of all on the mitigating circumstances and they took a different view on the appellant's role in the offence. So that even if the Nikolic rule does apply in this particular case, in this case, as in Nikolic, that standard has been met. On the first part of the argument, as to whether the Trial Chamber must state findings of fact on disputed matters, what I think the common theme with the four areas that have been identified is it all comes back to paragraph 79, where the Trial Chamber states that his participation, the appellant's, was not as limited as the parties suggest it was. I think if the Appeals Chamber looks at paragraph 79, you will see that they are citing there two undisputed matters of fact from elsewhere in the factual basis on the role that the appellant played in this joint criminal enterprise. Nowhere in this paragraph do they take issue with the facts earlier stated, that the -- there it was a parallel structure, that Mr. Babic was influenced by propaganda, and that Mr. Babic did not know at the time that they were occurring the scale and extent of the crimes. There is simply in there case, Your Honours, was no dispute between the parties on these particular factors and on these particular facts and therefore there was no need for the Trial Chamber to make findings of fact on these undisputed matters of fact. With that, Your Honours, I will conclude my submissions and open myself to questions, if you have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There are no questions, Counsel. Thank you very much for your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ten minutes reply by the appellant, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: First I just want to -- I'm sorry, very briefly, Your Honours, first I'd like to correct a factual error. My colleague stated that Mr. Babic testified at trial. In fact he testified at two trials, Milosevic and Krajisnik. With respect to the substantial diversion, it's two years of a man's life. At least. Under 11 -- I mean, I don't know how you gauge substantial. Does have to 50 per cent? Is it enough if it's 15 or 20 per cent? It's two years of a man's life. My colleague spoke to you about the Trial Chamber finding Mr. Babic in a leadership role for an aggravating circumstance, because of the office he held. If that reasoning holds, then anyone who is indicted, who is in a high political office no matter what their role in the joint criminal enterprise must be given an aggravating circumstance. Is that what the law intends? Or does the law intend that a person be given an aggravating circumstance for a leadership role if they in fact take a leadership role in the joint criminal enterprise? And that, I think, is the gravamen of the issue which I respectfully submit is undecided by the Appeals Chamber. Indeed, there have been cases where people in high political offices have been found to warrant the aggravating circumstance, but they were also leaders of the joint criminal enterprise. Here we have the unique situation where someone held high political office, but by the statements in the factual basis, and it's conceded, was not a leader in the joint criminal enterprise. That's the issue that I believe you must deal with. Thank you. Unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see no questions, Counsel. Thank you very much for your submissions. Sorry, Judge Guney has some question for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to seek some clarification on one point, which I find difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat. Yes, I would like to seek some clarification on a point that I find difficult to understand. In the appeals brief, you mentioned for the first time that Mr. Babic attempted to alleviate or to -- the problems prevailing in detention centres by using professional prison personnel, but you do not explain to what extent this contributed to improving detention conditions. Could you expand on this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: One moment, please. Your Honour, it's my understanding that at some point, Mr. Babic brought in new guards and was able to get rid of the brutality that was in there. Am I correct, Mr. Babic? Yes? When -- I would have no objection, Your Honour, if you would address this question to Mr. Babic. I believe he's probably better qualified to answer it than I am, with my apologies. But that is the basis of it, that he brought in new guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOGELNEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. There are no more questions. I now turn to the appellant, Mr. Milan Babic, if he wishes to address the Appeals Chamber, for ten minutes, please. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The only thing that I would like to say is that I'm very concerned for the safety of my family. I spoke about this earlier at previous Status Conferences and nothing has changed in that regard so far. This is the only thing that is important to me; nothing else but that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milan Babic. You may sit down. We have now come to the end of these proceedings. I wish to thank counsel for the appellant and counsel for the Prosecution and all the supporting staff for assisting the Court. The Court now stands adjourned.
